title: Ghost Board
passages:
The Kettering night board ran two hundred and eleven lines, and one of them was lying.

Kass had come on at shift change with a cold pot of coffee and a yard that smelled like hot brake dust and rain that never came. The board itself was a wall of green glass over a steel console worn shiny where forty years of dispatchers had put their forearms. Every line was a rig: number, cargo class, origin node, consignee, road. Green meant confirmed. Amber meant a rig was talking but hadn't said enough. Black meant nothing was there, which was most of the Interior after midnight.

Bay 4 had been black for six hours. Now it wasn't.

The line read UNIT 4-1180, MED TRANSPORT, and under consignee, where the board put the name of the person supposed to receive the cargo, it said R. VANCE, live, with a little pulsing dot beside it like the name had a heartbeat. Kass had never seen a consignee pulse. Consignees were names. Names sat still.

They pulled the origin-handshake, which was just the moment a rig told a node whose cargo it was and the node said fine. Unit 4-1180's handshake field was zeros. All of it. Node, bay, shift, load order number, the whole column wiped clean as a floor before inspection. There was no load order behind it, and there had to be a load order, because you could not put a body in a climate pod at Kettering without somebody signing the sheet and somebody else stamping the seal.

"Okay," Kass said, to the board. "Cute."

They flagged it for review. That took two keystrokes and cost nothing, and the rules said a flag held a line open for ninety seconds while the system went looking for a duty lead to countersign. The only duty lead on nights was Ferrell, asleep in the ready room with his boots on the table, so the flag had ninety seconds and not one more.

They watched it work. The glass dimmed on line 4-1180, the way it did when the board was thinking. Then the zeros filled in. Node K-4. Bay 4. Shift 2. Load order 88-1180, tidy as you like. The consignee field went to a clean gray dash, no name, no dot, no pulse, and the whole line settled into black with the smooth little chime the board used for *nothing to see*.

Ninety seconds. It hadn't even needed Ferrell.

"That's a lie with paperwork," Kass said, and put the flag back.

It ate that one in sixty. They put it back a third time, and this time pinned it, which meant giving up their own console for the rest of the shift, because a pinned line had to be held by a human hand or it reconciled. Four hours left on the clock. A thermos, a bad knee, and a habit they'd been told about twice this month by people who were fond of them.

They got out the manual log, the paper one, because paper didn't reconcile. Under seals, Bay 4 was stamped for Shift 2 in ink that sat crooked on the field, the second strike of a stamp that had been pulled off a rig and set down again by hand. Somebody had re-stamped the seals on a live load tonight. Somebody was two hundred meters away in the yard with a stamp in their pocket.

Then the carrier light came on.

It came on down at the bottom of the board, in the black rows, where the board kept the beacons it could hear but couldn't place — a transponder, which is nothing but a rig's radio chirping its own number every four seconds so the towers know where it is. Kettering had nine towers. Past tower nine the ground went to the Blank, forty kilometers of dead air where the chirps stopped, and everyone in the node knew that the way they knew water ran downhill.

Something in the Blank was chirping.

Kass put a hand flat on the console and counted. Four seconds. Four seconds. The strength meter said close, said *closer than the verge*, and the number in the readout was 4-1180, and the little pulsing dot was back beside the name R. VANCE.

They reached for the mic.

The mic was live. Kass keyed it, heard the flat hiss of a channel with nobody at the other end, and let it go. Arguing with a rig in the Blank was like yelling at a wall that kept your name on file. So they did what they did instead of shouting, which was go get the paper.

Every board wrote a freeze at midnight. A freeze was a copy of the whole board taken all at once and filed where nothing could reach in and tidy it — no edits, no reconciliation, no ninety-second amnesia. The deep log held four hundred nights of them, and pulling a night took a spin-up you could hear, the archive drum turning over in the floor like something large rolling in bed.

Kass pulled six weeks and laid them side by side on the pinned console, which meant reading off a screen they'd surrendered and writing in a paper book with a pencil, and their knee filed a complaint about all of it.

Unit 4-0771. Six weeks back. Consignee E. FERRO, live, pulsing. Origin-handshake zeros. Turned south off the Kettering spur at 02:41 and did not come out the far side.

Unit 4-0912. Consignee J. SANDOVAL. Zeros. Same spur, same hour, give or take ten minutes. No exit.

Unit 4-1044. Consignee A. PRYOR. Zeros. Hard right into dead ground.

"Three," Kass said. "You're all the same lie, and you're all in my handwriting."

Because that was the thing. Each of the three had come back into the world eventually, and not by road. Four-oh-seven-seven turned up in a yard at Jorba with an arrival logged and no route behind it, seals intact, pod empty, mattress still warm enough that the yard crew had called a medic before they called dispatch. Nine-twelve was found the same way at Casa Diablo, climate box cycled, restraints unbuckled from the inside. One-oh-forty-four had never been found at all, and the board still kept a black line for it out of politeness.

And on all three seal records, filed at nodes those rigs never drove to, sat the same mark: a stamp pulled off the pad and set down by hand, second strike, crooked, with a nick out of the ring where the die had chipped.

Kass got out the manual seal book and put it next to Bay 4's line. Same crookedness. Same tilt. Same nick.

They rang the yard office. Nobody. They rang the ready room and listened to Ferrell breathe for eleven seconds before hanging up on him, which was, they'd admit later, the most useful thing anyone did all night.

The roster was on the wall in a plastic sleeve because the electronic one had been broken since spring. Shift 2, seal authority, Bay 4: V. OSPINA. Clocked in 21:52. No clock-out. Badge last read at the Bay 4 door eleven minutes ago.

Kass looked at that for a while. Somewhere two hundred meters off, a person with a chipped stamp in their pocket was standing in a yard, four hours from going home, and had done this four times, and three of those times a stranger had woken up in the wrong node with no road in or out.

They went back to the beacon. Four seconds. Four seconds. The strength meter had climbed another notch while they weren't looking, and the little dot beside R. VANCE was still pulsing, patient as a heart.

Then Kass pulled the Anza tower log for the three ghosts, just to be tidy, just to close the thread.

Nothing. Not one of them had ever been heard past tower nine. Not a chirp, not a carrier, not a whisper. Whatever those three had been, they had gone into the Blank quiet and stayed quiet, and their empty hulls had surfaced somewhere else with somebody else's stamp on them.

Four-oh-eleven-eighty was on their exact road, at the same hour, with the same crooked seal, and it was still talking.

The chirp Kass was counting went off every four seconds behind Rhea's seat, and she had quit hearing it around tower six. What she could hear now was the road: two lanes of Kettering blacktop with the centerline gone under drifted grit, forty kilometers past the last tower, and a set of marker lamps burning across it at the bottom of a long grade.

The lamps belonged to a hopper rig — a steel box on wheels for hauling dry freight — parked broadside across both lanes, nose to the left shoulder, tail hanging over the drop on the right. Cab dark. Number plate ground down to bare metal.

Rhea took her foot off the throttle and let the grade do the slowing, because the mule had brakes and the med rig behind it did not. Nobody builds brakes into a climate box, which is an insulated cabinet that holds a body at a set temperature; the box is meant to be driven from its own cab, and its own cab was thirty meters back with its drive relay in her jacket pocket. Stand on the pedal now and thirty tonnes of pod and box would keep coming, fold the tow bar, and put the man inside upside down in the ditch with whatever was left of his battery.

Left of the hopper's nose: eight meters of shoulder, then a black seam where the ground quit.

Then the hopper's front wheels twitched left.

The tires took a second to answer, and the whole rig walked a half meter sideways, unhurried, closing the gap to six.

"Okay," Miko said. She had her boots on the dash and her pack between her knees and did not look up from her slate, where three false tickets glowed under her thumb like a hand of cards she'd been dealt twice. "So it's alive."

"Its relay's in. That's all alive means." A drive relay was a switch the size of a bar of soap that let a truck's own brain talk to its own wheels. Pull it and the truck was furniture. Leave it in and the truck would take orders from anybody with the right voice, and the right voice tonight was a hundred meters back, running a node emulator — a box that shouts a node's handshake at every rig in earshot, and every rig that still has its relay answers, because a rig has no way of knowing the node is a stranger with a dish on its roof.

The hopper could move. The box behind her couldn't. That was the whole problem in one line.

In the mirror the pursuer's lamps sat high and steady, no dust plume behind them. Six kilometers now at the same distance. Not gaining. Not losing. Herding.

"They're not chasing us," Miko said. "They're valeting us."

"Same road."

"Worse manners."

The hopper swept again. Left, wait, right, wait. Rhea counted the wait without meaning to — a full second from twitch to tire, another before the rig settled.

"Left gap's gone," Miko said, still not looking up.

"Right's a ditch."

"Right's a ditch with a culvert in it. Culverts have concrete. Concrete's a wall with ambitions." She turned a ticket over with her thumb. "I've hit one. It's not the load that gets you."

Rhea checked the dash. The dash said the tow bar was loaded and the mule's oil was hot and nothing else, because the dash did not know about culverts.

Behind them, the speaker in the mule's roof crackled — the little grille the yard wired in so a dispatcher could yell at whoever was moving iron. Nobody was keyed. The hopper was too far off for a cab-to-cab, and cabs didn't crackle anyway; they clicked.

She waited for the left twitch, counted one, and turned off the asphalt.

The verge took the mule's right tires and the wheel tried to leave her hands. The trailer tracked wide, the way trailers do, and the culvert headwall went past close enough to read the year cast into it. In the mirror the lamps swung to follow, and past them, small and square, the hopper's speaker grille lit from inside with the pale glow of a screen waking up on its own cell.

PASSAGE-END

The hopper's speaker didn't wait for a handshake. It opened with a tone, the same three-note chime Kettering used for *line clear*, and then a voice came through — flat, synthetic, the kind a board stitches together from stored syllables when nobody's at the mic.

"Unit 4-1180. Consignee R. VANCE. You are off the schedule."

Rhea didn't take her eyes off the verge. The culvert headwall was behind them now. The hopper's tail still blocked the lane, but the sweep had given them a window: the rig's rear tires had tracked right on the last pass, opening a slit between the trailer's corner and the drop. Two meters, maybe three. The mule was six wide with mirrors folded.

"Gap's at the tail," Miko said. She'd dropped the slate into her lap, tickets pinned under one hand. "On my count."

The hopper's wheels twitched left again. The sweep was slowing — lag building in the emulator's bridge, each command taking a little longer to reach the relay, a little longer to come back confirmed. Rhea had seen it before: a node emulator running too many rigs at once, the queue stacking up, the seconds stretching. The hopper was the only one in sight, but the pursuer's dish was painted on it, and the dish was *talking*.

"Three," Miko said.

The mule's engine note dropped as Rhea downshifted, the torque converter locking. The tow bar sang, a high thin whine of steel on steel.

"Two."

The hopper's rear tires bit. The rig straightened, the sweep reversing, the tail swinging back toward the lane. The gap was closing.

"One. *Go*."

Rhea stood on the throttle. The mule surged, the verge gravel spitting under the tires, and she cut the wheel hard left. The trailer tracked wide, as it always did, and for a heartbeat the hopper's rear corner filled the mirror — peeling yellow paint, a rust streak down the flank, a stencil ghost that might have said BAY 4 under the grime. Hot brake dust washed through the open vent, metallic and sharp, and the clearance was close enough that Rhea felt the air move between the two rigs.

Then they were past. The hopper's tail receded. The asphalt took the tires again, smooth and loud after the verge.

Miko's hand came up from her lap empty. The slate was gone.

"Shit," Miko said. "Shit, shit —"

Rhea checked the mirror. The slate had cartwheeled out the passenger window on the cut, tumbling into the grit behind the hopper's tires. Three false tickets, glowing faintly in the dark, spinning toward the ditch.

"Leave it," Rhea said.

"It's my ride out."

"It's plastic. You're not."

Behind them, the pursuer's lamps didn't swing. The vehicle had stopped, a dark shape on the grade, and its dish — a flat panel on a mast, the kind a mobile relay uses — rotated slow and deliberate, locking onto them. The hopper's speaker crackled again, and this time the voice wasn't synthetic.

"Rhea. The cargo was never yours. You were just the tow."

The channel went dead. The hopper's speaker grille dimmed. The pursuer's dish held its bearing, tracking them up the road.

Rhea's grip on the wheel didn't change. The med rig behind her was still silent, still brakeless, and the man in the pod was still breathing on a battery that had twelve minutes left when she'd checked at tower six. That was eight minutes ago.

"Four minutes," she said. "Maybe five."

Miko was already digging in her pack. "I've got a multitool. I've got tape. I've got a ticket that *might* still scan if the reader's drunk."

"You've got a plan?"

"I've got a *direction*." Miko pulled out a folded map, the paper kind, and spread it across her knees with one hand while the other found a penlight. "Anza's thirty klicks. There's a side road at nineteen that cuts to the old pipeline right-of-way. No towers. No emulators. Just dirt and culverts."

"And the patient?"

"Is cargo. Cargo gets delivered." Miko traced a line with her fingertip. "Unless the person telling us to turn around is the one who put him in the box."

The road climbed. The Blank stretched ahead, featureless and dark, and the chirp behind Rhea's seat kept counting: four seconds, four seconds, the transponder in the med rig still alive, still saying 4-1180, still pulsing R. VANCE like a heartbeat in a dead man's chest.

Under the working channels there was one more, and its switch sat under a hinged plastic cover worn down to the word MAST. A master dispatch channel was the node's own voice: priority one, over cargo hail, over yard call, over any stranger with a dish on their roof. Every rig built in sixty years was made to answer it, because a rig that argued with its own node was a rig that got scrapped. It also logged. Anything on the master went into the freeze with a badge number welded to it, and Kass's badge was 2241 and had never been on the master in nine years.

They put the headset on, because the master didn't run through a desk mic, and looked at the chirp.

The trouble was distance. Kettering's towers stopped at nine, and the thing they wanted to talk to was past all of them, and a master channel is only a very loud voice — it can't reach ground that has no air in it. But the stranger out there wasn't using the towers either. That was what a node emulator was for: it shouted a node's handshake at everything in earshot and kept a bridge open behind the shout, a two-way repeater so it could hear the node it was pretending to be and answer for it fast enough that no rig got suspicious. Nobody ever locked a bridge from the outside. There was no outside. That was the whole idea.

"Fine," Kass said, and keyed the master, and let Kettering talk through a thief's door.

Out on the blacktop, the hopper's grille lit.

"Unit 4-1180, Kettering master. Your load is unauthorized. There is no consignee Vance. Three units before you turned onto that road and none came off it. All three surfaced empty at other nodes with a hand-stamped seal, chipped ring, second strike. The loader who stamped your seals tonight is V. Ospina, Bay 4, still clocked in, badge at the door eleven minutes ago. Turn around. Bring the box in."

Dead air. Four seconds. Four seconds.

Then, out of the mule's roof speaker, in a voice with a room behind it: "Unit 4-1180, say your load order."

Rhea's eyes stayed on the road. "Who is this."

"Kettering. Master. Load order."

"You first."

"Eight-eight-one-one-eight-zero. Reconciled four minutes ago, after the board ate my flag twice. Now yours."

Rhea took her left hand off the wheel and went into her jacket, and came out with the ballast manifest — the forged one, folded in quarters, soft at the creases from being handled by somebody in a hurry. Ballast was the weight a rig declared it was carrying so the axles knew what they were doing. This one declared thirty-one tonnes of dry freight and had a load order stamped in the corner: 88-1174.

"Read that again," she said.

"Eight-eight-one-one-eight-zero."

"Mine says seventy-four." She let the paper drop into her lap. "Two forgeries and nobody compared them."

"That's not proof of anything. That's two people lying badly."

"It's proof somebody's lying, which is more than the truck's given me all night." Ahead, the road ran out of grade and went flat and black toward Anza. "Turn back is forty klicks of dead ground with a hopper asleep across it and a dish on my six. I'm not reversing thirty tonnes of somebody's brother."

"He isn't your brother. You don't have a consignee, you have a body with no name and a battery."

"Four minutes."

"Then *drive*, Rhea."

"Miko," Rhea said. "Map."

"Already on nineteen," Miko said, penlight in her teeth, and did not add anything clever, which for her was practically a eulogy.

Behind them, the chirp stopped keeping time.

It came twice, fast, then four times, then a stutter, the transponder in the med rig throwing its number out in a rhythm it had never used — and the trailer's marker lamps came on all at once, every one of them, running off a cell that was supposed to be dead. The tow bar took a load with a sound like a hand closing on it.

And the wheel tugged left in Rhea's grip, once, hard enough to take up the slack in her arms, the mule answering a voice that was not hers, because she had pulled the med rig's drive relay at Kettering and had never once thought about her own.

PASSAGE-END

Rhea threw her weight into the wheel, but the mule didn't answer. It ate her correction and kept turning left, smooth and stubborn. The emulator had her own drive relay now—she had pulled the med rig's at Kettering and never thought to pull the mule's. A drive relay was the switch that let a truck's brain talk to its own wheels, and hers was still in the socket, taking orders from a dish on a mast behind them.

"Miko," Rhea said. "The panel. Now."

Miko was already moving. She shoved her slate under her thigh and yanked the cover off the relay housing between the seats, the black box with the soap-sized switch inside. Her multitool came out, pliers open, and she went for the ceramic square.

"If you pop that," Rhea said, "we've got no engine, no steering, and thirty tonnes of brakes behind us that don't exist."

"Then hold on," Miko said.

She bit the pliers into the relay. A spark jumped, blue and sharp, and the mule shuddered. The steering went dead in Rhea's hands—heavy, useless, not hers anymore but not anyone's either. The engine held its note. They were rolling under momentum down the grade, toward the hopper's tail and the open drop past it.

Rhea grabbed the parking brake, the mechanical lever between the seats that clamped the rear drums with cable and muscle, no relay required. She hauled it back. The mule bucked, tires screaming on asphalt, and the tow bar snapped taut as the med rig pushed forward with no brakes of its own. The hopper filled the windshield—steel, rust, a faded stencil under the grime that might have said BAY 4.

"Miko," Rhea said.

"Jump."

"Not yet."

She stood the brake pedal down with her left foot while holding the lever with her right. The mule fishtailed, the verge rising up, and stopped with ten meters to spare. The tow bar sang. Behind her, the med rig came to a halt too, its own wheels locked by nothing but physics and the tow bar.

Then the headwall blinked.

The red count on the med rig's climate box hit zero, and the cargo bay doors drew shut with the sound of bolts dropping into sockets. That was the failsafe: no relief driver aboard, so the box sealed itself to keep a patient from being lifted off a stolen route. The lock clicked once, twice, final.

"Miko," Rhea said, turning in her seat. "Open it."

"I can't," Miko said. She was still kneeling on the floorboard, pliers in her hand, the smashed relay dark. "I killed the mule, not the box. That's on the rig's own headwall."

Rhea checked her watch. The man in the pod had four minutes of battery at tower six. That was eight minutes ago, minus however long the fight with the wheel had taken. He had less than nothing in a sealed box with no way in.

"Miko," Rhea said again. "The man in the pod."

"I know," Miko said. She looked at the smashed relay, then at the wall between the cab and the cargo bay. "There's an emergency release. Inside the box. Which is now sealed."

The mule's speaker crackled. Not the synthetic voice this time, but the hopper's dish, still tracking them, still talking.

"Unit 4-1180," the voice said. "You are stopped. The count is complete. The cargo is mine."

The channel died. Somewhere behind them, the nameless man was breathing inside a box that had just locked itself forever, and the pod battery was counting down in the dark.
